clue.text: Earth, what goes around the sun

indicators.note: going around means turning back on itself, so the two pieces before it are read backwards

parts.note: earth is soil, the ground
eh is a 'what?' asking someone to repeat themselves

explanation.surface: A schoolroom question: what is the thing that circles the sun? Earth.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites Earth as the answer to 'what goes around the sun', but Earth is a piece of wordplay and 'goes around' turns both pieces backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Helios is the Greek god and personification of the sun, so the name stands for it.

clue.text: Cups turning up in time for port

indicators.note: in places the reversed cups piece within the time piece

parts.note: an hour is a unit of time

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the cups word from bottom to top

parts.note: a bra is a garment of cups

explanation.surface: Teacups are lifted just in time for a glass of port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' looks like the drink after the cups, but here it means a place where ships shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: A port is a sheltered place where ships dock, which is what a harbour is.

clue.text: All finally on reel, you mean, filming Bambi — it's a wrap!

indicators.note: All finally takes the closing letter of every one of the words reel, you, mean, filming and Bambi

explanation.surface: A director wrapping up the shoot of Bambi declares the film finished: 'it's a wrap!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'All' looks like a word to be used, but 'All finally' means the last letter of each word after 'on'. 'it's a wrap' is the film-set cry, but literally describes a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A lungi is a cloth wrapped round the waist, worn in South Asia, so it is literally a wrap.

clue.text: Stumbling into us, head of government having entered, trips

indicators.note: having entered says the leading government letter goes inside the jumbled letters
stumbling suggests the letters of into us falling about into a new order
head of takes the first letter of government

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles into us just as the head of government comes in: a series of trips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stumbling' rearranges INTO US to OUTINS, and 'having entered' puts G inside. 'trips' looks like stumbles but means excursions.
explanation.definitionFit: Outings are short excursions or jaunts, which is the sense of trips as journeys.

clue.text: Quickly get ahead after game

indicators.note: after places the ahead word following the game word

parts.note: snap is a children's card game
up means ahead, as in a team being two goals up

explanation.surface: A competitor gets an early lead after a game.
explanation.walkthrough: SNAP is a card game in which players shout 'snap' on matching cards.
explanation.definitionFit: To snap up a bargain is to seize it eagerly before anyone else can.

clue.text: See 6
Neptune: a ball in pieces circling a remarkably hollow luminous cloud

indicators.note: circling says the jumbled letters ring round the second a and the hollowed word
in pieces says Neptune, a and ball are broken up and reassembled
hollow empties out remarkably, leaving only its outer letters

explanation.surface: Neptune, a gas giant, shattered and surrounded by a remarkably empty glowing cloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in pieces' splits the jumble into two words that sit either side of A plus the outer letters of 'remarkably'; 'circling' places them round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A planetary nebula is the glowing shell of gas thrown off by a dying star, an astronomical cloud.

clue.text: Extra fat bear has lost weight

indicators.note: has lost says the weight word is removed from the bear's name

parts.note: Paddington is the marmalade-loving bear of children's books
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A rather plump bear has slimmed down.
explanation.walkthrough: PADDINGTON is the children's book bear from Peru found at a London railway station; take TON away.
explanation.definitionFit: Padding is surplus material, so extra fat on a body is jokingly called padding.

clue.text: Spun thing, as gripped by mercurial spinners, say?

indicators.note: gripped by puts the twisted letters inside the mercurial word

parts.note: mercurial means changeable, fickle

indicators.note: spun suggests the letters of thing and as being whirled into a new order

explanation.surface: A thing spun round and held by unpredictable spin bowlers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spun' signals the anagram. Spinners suggest cricket bowlers, but they are revolving lures; '?' marks them as an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinners are revolving lures used by anglers, one kind of the gear for catching fish.

clue.text: What one might say after fleeing country

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I, and also the speaker saying 'I'
fleeing means running away, so having fled one would say ran

explanation.surface: The words a person would utter after running away.
explanation.walkthrough: Someone who has fled would say 'I ran'; run together it gives the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Iran is a nation in western Asia, formerly Persia.

clue.text: Platforms attached to lorries, those managing to go in reverse

parts.note: the reverse of a coin is its tail side
boards are the bodies of directors that manage companies

explanation.surface: Company directors trying to back their trucks up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverse' suggests driving backwards, but it is the tail side of a coin; 'to go in' merely joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Tailboards are the hinged back panels of lorries that drop down to form a loading platform.

clue.text: Juice knocked back with endless food from another planet

indicators.note: knocked back reads the juice abbreviation backwards, as well as suggesting gulping a drink

parts.note: OJ is short for orange juice

indicators.note: endless cuts the final letter from the food word

parts.note: viand is an old word for an item of food

explanation.surface: Someone gulps juice with a never-ending meal of alien cuisine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' looks like drinking, but it turns OJ into JO; VIAND loses its end to give VIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Jovian means relating to the planet Jupiter, so it describes something from a planet other than ours.

clue.text: Greek woman in Paris punches chin furiously

indicators.note: punches has the French woman driven into the jumbled chin letters
furiously suggests the letters of chin thrown about wildly

parts.note: elle is French for she, a woman

explanation.surface: A Greek woman in Paris lands angry blows on someone's chin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'furiously' scrambles the chin letters, and 'punches' drives the French 'she' into them, just after their first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hellenic is the formal adjective for things of Greece and its people.

clue.text: Abstract making leverage to impress European Commission leaders

indicators.note: to impress means to press into, so the leading letters are pushed inside the leverage word

parts.note: prising is levering something open

indicators.note: leaders takes the first letter of European and of Commission

explanation.surface: An abstract document using leverage to sway the heads of the European Commission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abstract' looks like a noun or an adjective, but here it is the verb, to summarise.
explanation.definitionFit: To précis a text is to summarise it, which is to abstract its main points.

clue.text: Constellation where Uranus etc misplaced

indicators.note: misplaced says the letters of Uranus and etc are put in the wrong positions

explanation.surface: An astronomer wonders which constellation Uranus and co have wandered off to.
explanation.definitionFit: Centaurus, the centaur, is a large southern constellation containing Alpha Centauri.

clue.text: Smack fly on the rebound

indicators.note: on the rebound means bouncing back, so the fly word is read backwards

parts.note: a gnat is a small fly

explanation.surface: Swatting a fly that bounces back off a window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' looks like a blow, but it means a flavour, as in 'smacks of'.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack is a distinctive taste or trace, and a tang is a sharp, distinctive flavour.

clue.text: Flag adopted by Bantus in Kenya

indicators.note: adopted by says the word is taken in and held within the following words

explanation.surface: A national flag taken up by Bantu peoples living in Kenya.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' looks like a banner, but it is the verb meaning to weaken.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to tire or droop, and to sink is to decline or lose strength.

clue.text: Mars visited by leader from Epsom, a town in Surrey

indicators.note: visited by puts the Epsom letter inside the Mars word, as a visitor comes in

parts.note: to mar is to spoil, and stains spoil things

indicators.note: leader from takes the first letter of Epsom

explanation.surface: The planet Mars receives a visit from a leading figure from Epsom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mars' looks like the planet, but it is the verb meaning spoils. Epsom and Staines are both towns in Surrey, a county south-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Staines, now Staines-upon-Thames, is a town on the Thames in Surrey.

clue.text: Old cop, having secured lighter and ciggy in the end, lights up on a clear night

definitions.text: lights up on a clear night

indicators.note: having secured says the old cop holds the end letters inside him

parts.note: Starsky is one of the two detectives in the 1970s American TV series Starsky and Hutch

indicators.note: in the end takes the last letter of lighter and of ciggy

explanation.surface: A retired policeman grabs his lighter and cigarette and lights up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lights up' suggests lighting a cigarette, but it is the stars filling the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: On a cloudless night the heavens are lit by stars, so the starlit heavens are what lights up.

clue.text: Beastly male duck, flipping fast

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep, a beast

indicators.note: flipping turns the duck word over, reading it backwards

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, nada

explanation.surface: A male animal and a duck turning over in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' looks like quick, but it is a period of not eating.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramadan is the Muslim month of daytime fasting, so it is itself a fast.

clue.text: By the sound of it, money only for a subcontinental area

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the words that follow are heard rather than spelt

parts.note: cash is money and mere means only, giving cash mere

explanation.surface: Someone sounds as though they care about nothing but cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Kashmir is a disputed region in the north of the Indian subcontinent.

clue.text: Tailor finished off dressing butt

indicators.note: dressing means clothing, so the finished-off word wraps around the butt word

parts.note: to finish off food is to eat it all, so ate
a butt is a large cask, as is a tun

explanation.surface: A tailor completes a garment covering someone's bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailor' looks like the dressmaker, but it is the verb meaning adapt. 'butt' is a cask, not a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: To tailor something is to adjust it to fit, and to attune is to bring it into harmony.

clue.text: Extremely big girl, very cold having left boozer finally

parts.note: gal is an informal word for girl

indicators.note: having left says the boozer letter departs from the very cold word

parts.note: arctic means extremely cold

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of boozer

explanation.surface: A large girl, frozen stiff after leaving the pub at closing time.
explanation.walkthrough: A boozer is British slang for a pub; its last letter R leaves ARCTIC, giving ACTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Galactic means on the scale of a galaxy, and so is used for anything enormously vast.

clue.text: Saturnine flash on Venus, for example

parts.note: mo is short for moment, as in 'in a flash'
Venus, a planet, is something that rose in the sky, so the planet in action gives rose

explanation.surface: An astronomer spots a gloomy flash of light on the planet Venus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saturnine' looks planetary, but means gloomy; Venus rises as the morning star, hence ROSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturnine describes a sullen, gloomy temperament, which is what morose means.

clue.text: Top, top game

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so the first letter of the game word goes

parts.note: bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: A bare-bones exchange: the top choice is the best game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top' is used twice: first as the noun for a crest, then as the verb meaning to behead.
explanation.definitionFit: A ridge is the crest or highest line of a hill or roof, its top.

clue.text: Drained after tight run-out, remaining calm

indicators.note: after places the drained word following the jumbled letters
tight is slang for drunk, which suggests the letters of run-out reeling about

parts.note: bled means drained of blood

explanation.surface: A batsman stays calm after a close run-out leaves him exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tight' looks like a close call, but it means drunk, reshuffling RUNOUT into UNTROU. A run-out is a way a batsman is dismissed in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone untroubled is undisturbed by worry, which is the state of keeping one's composure.

clue.text: Dark energy ready for NASA?

parts.note: dim means dark, poorly lit
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Is the mysterious dark energy ready for the space agency to study?
explanation.walkthrough: 'ready' is British slang for cash; NASA stands in for America, where a dime is a coin, hence the '?'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dime is a ten-cent American coin, so it is cash as the USA would know it.

clue.text: Stop following characters central to sissyish arrangement

indicators.note: following places the stop word after the central letters
central to picks the two middle letters of sissyish

parts.note: to stem a flow is to stop it

explanation.surface: Someone stops characters behaving in an effeminate way.
explanation.definitionFit: A system is an organised scheme, an ordered arrangement of parts.

clue.text: Draw in boundary, one cut off by post-impressionist

parts.note: an end is a boundary or limit
Van Gogh, the post-impressionist painter, famously cut off his own ear

explanation.surface: A painter sketches inside a border, then a post-impressionist slices one away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' suggests painting, but 'Draw in' means attract.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw someone in is to win their affection, which is what endearing yourself to them does.
